issue.body:
## Overview

Tag vLLM wheels `cp311-abi3` instead of `cp38-abi3`, and make the release install snippets look up the wheel URL instead of hardcoding the filename.

## Claims

- The `cp38-abi3` tag is wrong: `spinloop` and `fs_io_C` import stable-ABI symbols added in Python 3.10 and 3.11. `requires-python = ">=3.11"` keeps this harmless for installers, but the tag should say 3.11.
- The release install snippets hardcode the wheel filename, including `cp38-abi3`, so they'd break with the new tag. They now look the URL up from the release's assets, which works for both tags. (The CPU snippets also currently point at `manylinux_2_34`, but v0.31.0 ships `manylinux_2_39`; see #58270.)

## Validation

`abi3audit` on the published v0.31.0 CPU x86 wheel (`vllm-0.31.0+cpu-cp38-abi3-manylinux_2_39_x86_64.whl`):

| Extension | Needs | Symbols newer than 3.8 |
|---|---|---|
| `spinloop.abi3.so` | 3.11 | `PyBuffer_Release` (3.11), `PyObject_CallNoArgs` (3.10) |
| `fs_io_C.abi3.so` | 3.11 | `PyBuffer_Release`, `PyObject_GetBuffer` (3.11), `PyUnicode_AsUTF8AndSize` (3.10) |
| `_C`, `_C_AVX2`, `_C_AVX512`, `_rust_tool_parser` | 3.8 | none |

- A CPU wheel built from this branch (macOS arm64, `setup.py bdist_wheel --py-limited-api=cp311`) is named `...-cp311-abi3-...whl`, and `abi3audit` reports no mismatches.
- In the published v0.31.0 CUDA (x86_64) and XPU wheels, every abi3 extension (13 and 1) needs at most 3.11; only `spinloop` and `fs_io_C` need more than 3.8. The CUDA wheel also bundles DeepGEMM as per-version `_C.cpython-3{10..14}` builds, which this PR doesn't change.
- A CUDA wheel built from this branch on an A40 with `docker/Dockerfile`'s command (`setup.py bdist_wheel --py-limited-api=cp311`, using `VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1` to skip compiling) is named `...-cp311-abi3-linux_x86_64.whl` (CI's `detect-manylinux-tag.py` rewrites the platform tag later). `abi3audit` passes for all 13 extensions; the wheel installs into a clean Python 3.12 venv and its CUDA libraries load on the GPU; Python 3.10 refuses it via `requires-python`.
- The three doc snippets, run as written, resolve to existing assets for both `latest` (v0.31.0) and `tags/v0.30.0` (CPU x86_64, CPU aarch64, `+cu129` x86_64).
- Nothing in the release tooling depends on `cp38`: `generate-nightly-index.py` parses tags generically, `detect-manylinux-tag.py` only rewrites the platform tag, and the precompiled-wheel lookup in `setup.py` ignores the Python tag.

## Details

- `docker/Dockerfile` (3 places), `Dockerfile.cpu`, `Dockerfile.xpu`, `.buildkite/scripts/build-macos-wheel.sh`, and the usage comment in `tools/setup_deepgemm_pythons.sh`: `--py-limited-api=cp38` → `cp311`.
- `gpu.cuda.inc.md`, `cpu.x86.inc.md`, `cpu.arm.inc.md`: select the wheel from the latest release's assets with `jq` (the snippets already used the GitHub API for the version). A comment shows how to pin a release (`tags/v<version>`). The CUDA snippet's example `CUDA_VERSION=130` matches no asset, because 13.0 is the unsuffixed default wheel; that's unchanged from `main`, where the hardcoded URL 404s, and is left for a separate docs fix.
- `tools/build_rust.py`: the commented PyO3 template uses `abi3-py311`.
- Example filenames in `nightly_builds.md`, `setup.py` and `generate-nightly-index.py` describe already-published wheels and are left as is.
- The published macOS wheel is tagged `cp312-cp312` even though `build-macos-wheel.sh` passes the flag (a local macOS build with it is `cp311-abi3`). I haven't tracked down why; the script is updated only for consistency.
- Follow-up: ROCm, s390x, ppc64le and `.github/workflows/scripts/build.sh` don't pass the flag and are unchanged, so their wheels keep a per-version tag. Setting the tag once in `setup.py` would cover every build path, but it changes the ROCm wheel names, so it belongs with the ROCm owners.
- Compatibility: scripts that build release URLs with `cp38-abi3` in the filename (as the old docs did) will 404 for releases after this lands. Wheels found through PyPI or the nightly index are unaffected.

**Duplicate check.** No open PR changes the wheel tag or these install snippets.

issue.title: [Build] keep CUDA PyTorch wheels aligned with image

labels.name: ready
labels.description: ONLY add when PR is ready to merge/full CI is needed

issue.body:
## Summary

Fix stable CUDA Docker dependency resolution so the CUDA-specific PyTorch index is authoritative for PyTorch packages.

The Dockerfile previously passed the CUDA index as an extra index while the environment used `unsafe-best-match`. In a `cu129` build, that allowed dependency resolution to select a higher preinstalled Torch build from another source, producing the reported `torch 2.14.0+cu130` / `torchvision 0.28.0+cu129` mismatch and breaking `import torchvision`.

Stable CUDA install stages now use the CUDA index as the primary index, PyPI as the fallback for non-PyTorch packages, and `unsafe-first-match` so package resolution cannot silently substitute a different CUDA build. The change is applied consistently to base, build, test/dev, runtime, vLLM wheel, and extension install stages.

## Validation

- `git diff --check` passes.
- Resolved the CUDA requirements with uv's stable-index configuration for a Linux manylinux target; local execution of the full image is unavailable because the Docker daemon is not running.

Fixes #59157

issue.body: ## Summary This PR enables DeepSeek V4 Flash on SM120/SM121 Blackwell client hardware by carrying the SM12x fallback and tuning stack needed for the current vLLM V1 path. It targets RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition, RTX 5090-class SM120, and GB10 / DGX Spark SM121 users who cannot use SM100-only TMEM / `tcgen05` kernels. The branch is **reconciled on top of the merged #43477** and provides the **stock-deps path**: DeepSeek V4 on SM120/121 that builds and serves on *released* FlashInfer / DeepGEMM wheels, complementing #43477's route that needs the unreleased FlashInfer #3395 + DeepGEMM #324 dependency branches. It is kept **synced onto current `upstream/main`**. **Latest validated head: tag `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260809` (`aa0d513027`), synced onto `upstream/main` as of 2026-08-09 (`f18e10a7e1`)** — see [Update 2026-08-09](#update-2026-08-09) below. **The default model runner is now V2**; `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` still selects V1, which stays supported. **Model / speculative-decode status.** `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` is the checkpoint this branch is validated on. It **removed the MTP heads** and folded the DSpark draft into the main checkpoint, so **DSpark (`method: "dspark"`, `num_speculative_tokens: 5`) is the speculative path**; MTP is supported only for older checkpoints that still carry those weights. Running without speculation is also fully supported and validated. ## Change footprint — model kernels vs. core-vLLM touch points 187 files, ~+29.1k / −1.3k against `upstream/main`, of which ~10.7k added lines are tests. The branch splits cleanly into model/kernel code and a small set of core-vLLM integration points: - **DeepSeek-V4 model + SM12x kernels — the enablement itself.** Everything under `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/**` plus the SM12x sparse-MLA decode / indexer / DeepGEMM kernels that live in shared dirs (`v1/attention/backends/mla/sparse_mla_kernels.py`, `model_executor/layers/sparse_attn_indexer.py`, `v1/attention/backends/mla/{indexer,sparse_swa}.py`, `utils/deep_gemm.py`, `kernels/mhc/tilelang.py`), the new DSv4 reasoning parser / tokenizer, and device tuning JSONs. - **C128A metadata device→host sync removed** (`models/deepseek_v4/sparse_mla.py`, perf) — `_c128a_effective_topk_width` takes the max position from the CPU-side `CommonAttentionMetadata.max_seq_len` instead of a per-step `int(positions.max().item())` device sync, dropping a launch-stream stall on every C128A metadata step. Decode is identical (`max_seq_len-1 == positions.max()`); only chunked prefill sees a safe, slightly-wider 128-aligned top-k. - **Core-vLLM integration — the hooks below.** Almost all are gated by model architecture / quant config / an env flag and are inert for other models. | Subsystem | Files | What it does | | --- | --- | --- | | KV-cache core | `single_type_kv_cache_manager.py`, `kv_cache_coordinator.py`, `kv_cache_manager.py`, `sched/scheduler.py` (+1) | prefix-cache correctness for DSv4 sparse-MLA + speculative decode: an MLA cache-manager with prompt-block protection, a hybrid-coordinator `cache_blocks` tail-block-reuse rewrite | | Speculative decode | `v1/spec_decode/{dspark,dspark_sampling,llm_base_proposer,dflash}.py`, `config/speculative.py` | DSpark self-drafting proposer + sampling; DSv4 probabilistic draft sampling and per-step draft-layer routing in the shared proposer base; DSpark/MTP method detection and validation | | MoE quantization | `fused_moe.py`, `oracle/mxfp4.py`, `routed_experts.py`, `experts/flashinfer_cutlass_moe.py`, `quantization/mxfp4.py`, `oracle/nvfp4.py` | MXFP4 / NVFP4 backend selection; the one-line NVFP4 fix (FLASHINFER_CUTLASS into the SwiGLU-clamp allow-list) lets DSv4-Flash-NVFP4 serve | | FP8 / Marlin GEMM | `quantization/utils/fp8_utils.py`, `linear/scaled_mm/{cutlass,marlin}.py`, `csrc/.../marlin_moe_wna16/ops.cu` (the only C++) | SM12x e8m0→fp32 upcast + Marlin MoE SM12.0a cudagraph hardening | | cudagraph / compile / config | `config/vllm.py`, `compilation/breakable_cudagraph.py`, `passes/utility/fix_functionalization.py`, `config/compilation.py` | breakable-cudagraph auto-enable gate (MiniMax-only; DSv4 deliberately excluded), DSv4 custom-op defunctionalization + splitting-op registration | | OpenAI entrypoints / parsers | `chat_completion/protocol.py`, `serve/render/serving.py`, `tool_parsers/structural_tag_registry.py`, `chat_utils.py`, `engine/protocol.py`, `chat_completion/{serving,batch_serving}.py`, `reasoning/__init__.py` | expose DSv4 API semantics — `reasoning_content` / `thinking` param / tool-call streaming (jasl/vllm#19 instruction-following) | | Kernel warmup | `model_executor/warmup/deepseek_v4_sm12x_warmup.py` (new), `kernel_warmup.py` (+11) | DSv4 warmup passes (D512-split prefill precompile, paged-MQA rowwise, draft path) that avoid JIT-during-inference wedges. Kept in a separate module so `kernel_warmup.py` stays a two-line hook on upstream's file | | Weight loading | `weight_utils.py`, `default_loader.py` | fast-safetensors weight filter + EP-skip (lowers DSv4 load overhead on GB10) | | env / utils | `envs.py`, `utils/flashinfer.py`, `utils/import_utils.py`, `v1/worker/{gpu_model_runner,ubatch_utils}.py` | `VLLM_DEEPSEEK_V4_*` flags + `has_cutedsl` / `has_flashinfer_trtllm_sparse_mla` probes | Two notes for review: - The most invasive generic edits were **removed** in the 2026-06-21 audit cleanup: the scheduler carries a single +1-line change (the prefill-fairness heuristics were dropped) and the prefix-cache write-fence is gone. - A few hooks touch code paths shared with non-DSv4 models and are worth a closer look: the `kv_cache_coordinator` `cache_blocks` rewrite (affects hybrid-KV models; validated ≥ prior behavior), the proposer base-class change, and the OpenAI-entrypoint plumbing. Everything else (MoE oracle, fp8_utils, cudagraph gate, warmup, envs) is arch / quant / env-gated and inert for other models. ## Duplicate-work check The nearest open/merged PRs are related but not duplicates: | PR | Difference | | --- | --- | | #43477 | **Merged 2026-06-22.** Enables DeepSeek V4 + GLM-5.1 on SM120 via the FlashInfer-SM120 sparse-MLA route, but on its merged form **requires the unreleased FlashInfer #3395 + DeepGEMM #324 dependency branches** — on released/stock wheels its SM12x path raises at model construction. This PR is **reconciled on top of #43477** (merge `42657aca65`) and carries the **stock-deps** DSv4 SM120/121 path that runs on released wheels. | | #40929 | Earlier WIP Triton fallback effort. This PR is the maintained replacement branch with the broader scheduler, prefix-cache, parser, quant, warmup, and harness-validated fixes carried forward. | | #42856 | Focused workspace-bound fix that explicitly depends on / references this PR; a subset-style bugfix, not the full DeepSeek V4 SM12x enablement branch. | | #49335 | mxfp8 activation-scale swizzle after DP/EP dispatch — **carried in this branch** (unclaimed upstream). Inert at DP=1; taken for this branch's multi-node DP users. | | #50686 | Consecutive-assistant-message merging in DSv4 prompt encoding — **carried in this branch** (reproduced here before taking it). | | #50693 | B300-targeted prefill-workspace fix. **Test carried, code not needed**: this branch's `_prefill_workspace_topk_bound` returns early for `compress_ratio <= 1` and never reaches the affected buffer. | Upstream PRs whose fixes this branch previously carried as local deltas and has since **retired** in favour of upstream's own version: #48304, #48911, #48959 (via #49052). ## Fixed preview tags These tags are in `jasl/vllm` and give users stable pins while the PR is still moving: | Tag | Commit | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260809` | `aa0d513027` | **latest validated head** — 87 upstream commits incl. FlashInfer 0.6.16.post3; the V2 recall collapse root-caused as a prefix-cache ghost-block race and fixed (port of #42359); **default runner switched to V2**. See **Update 2026-08-09**. | | `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260804` | `0f59188db1` | 35 further upstream commits, four fixes from community reports (DSpark out-of-vocab draft token, eager scratch pool), two contributor PRs. Validated on **both** SM121 and SM120. See **Update 2026-08-04**. | | `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260802` | `9a94c54292` | 234 upstream commits, `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` support, two DSpark config fixes, #49335 / #50686 absorbed. See **Update 2026-08-02**. | | `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260727d` | `d64074e6f0` | 209-commit upstream sync + torch 2.13 (tag `…-20260727`, `70a33886bd`); DSpark VRAM work (jasl/vllm#27) merged; bounded block-table gather in `compute_global_topk_indices_and_lens`. | | `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260721` | `832775efd1` | 79-commit upstream sync; #48911 dropped in favour of upstream's merged version; compact CPU KV offload (opt-in). | | `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260717` | `f63bfd3d7b` | 195-commit upstream sync; prefill ctx_pp +4.7% @ d8192. | | `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260711` | `b5c0d43b96` | 181-commit upstream sync; #48304 MTP unscaled-draft-rope; ~1097-line dead-kernel cleanup. | | `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260704` | `b43470e871` | @GanyX19 GB10 fixes: per-shape `constexpr`→runtime (stops the Triton recompile → unified-memory leak → hard-freeze) + fp8-einsum `tl.multiple_of(16)` (~24% decode @256K). | | `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260703` | `444fe3ac8b` | DSpark spec-decode (self-drafting block-5), V2 padded-Q OOM fix (jasl/vllm#26), exact non-cooperative `persistent_topk` for <128 KB-smem parts. | Older tags (`…-20260705` back to `…-20260612…`) remain in `jasl/vllm` for history. ## Update 2026-08-02 — `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`, 234 upstream commits, two DSpark fixes Validated head **`9a94c54292`** (tag `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260802`), 234 upstream commits absorbed, level with `upstream/main` as of 2026-08-02. **What's in it** - **`DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` support.** The new checkpoint ships **no MTP heads** — `enorm`, `hnorm`, `e_proj`, `h_proj` and `shared_head` are absent from the weight index, and `mtp.{0,1,2}.*` now carries the DSpark-style `main_norm` / `main_proj` structure (matching `dspark_target_layer_ids: [40, 41, 42]`). DSpark is the speculative path going forward; the MTP code is retained for older checkpoints. - **`num_speculative_tokens` vs `dspark_block_size`** — *this rule was relaxed on 2026-08-04; see Update 2026-08-04. It now errors only BELOW the block size and warns above it.* The original reasoning and measurements follow. - The validator was tightened to require equality. The validator previously accepted `>=` and its error message recommended exceeding it. The drafter emits exactly one block per pass, so the extra slots are structurally unreachable — measured on a prose workload, the **7th draft position accepted 0.000 in every sample** (the 6th in all but one, 0.004 there), and `nst=7` drafts 40% more tokens per step for strictly worse acceptance: | configuration | mean acceptance length (3 samples) | avg draft acceptance rate | | --- | --- | --- | | nst=5 probabilistic | 2.15 / 2.16 / **2.19** | 22.9 / 23.2 / **23.8%** | | nst=7 probabilistic | 1.61 / 1.75 / 1.95 | 8.7 / 10.7 / 13.6% | | nst=5 greedy | 1.82 / 2.06 / **2.23** | 16.4 / 21.2 / **24.5%** | | nst=7 greedy | 1.57 / 1.66 / 1.75 | 8.2 / 9.5 / 10.8% | All samples are shown rather than a single figure: the probe reads whatever `SpecDecoding metrics` lines vLLM flushed inside its window, so a low sample means "not much steady traffic in that slice", not a worse drafter. Both `nst=7` runs also hit connection errors partway through, so their spread is noisier. - **`method: "mtp"` is no longer silently rewritten to `"dspark"`.** Auto-detection preserved an explicitly requested method only for `eagle`/`eagle3`/`dflash`/`dspark`. Since 0731 puts `dspark_block_size` in every DSv4 config, `method: "mtp"` fell through to the dspark branch, was rewritten, and then failed validation with a DSpark message the user never asked for. - **Absorbed** #49335 (mxfp8 activation-scale swizzle after DP/EP dispatch, verified non-vacuous) and #50686 (consecutive assistant messages merged in prompt encoding — it also removes a spurious mid-turn `<|end_of_sentence|>` on the default `drop_thinking=True` path). #50693's regression test is carried; its code fix is not reachable here. - **Three community reports re-tested and not reproduced** on this head: nst=7 draft-position collapse, TP=4 + expert-parallel `Check failed: num_tokens > 64`, and `FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV4` missing `tile_sched`. Details in [this comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41834#issuecomment-5152562124). **Validation (GB10 SM121, 2-node TP=2, `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`, torch 2.13.0, FlashInfer 0.6.15.post1, nccl 2.30.7)** | | DSpark nst=5 | no speculation | | --- | --- | --- | | GSM8K 8-shot (flexible) | 0.9394 | 0.9500 | | GSM8K 8-shot (strict) | 0.9363 | 0.9484 | | instruction-following (jasl/vllm#19, JSON-only) | PASS | PASS | | long-context recall (arthur needle, c=1) | 2/2 | 2/2 | | illegal-access / assertion in serve log | 0 | 0 | | draft acceptance (prose) | mean 2.08, 21.7% | — | The GSM8K difference (1.06 pp flexible / 1.21 pp strict) is within this gate's measured single-run spread (~1.1 pp). **Resolved:** three runs per cell were collected and the arms interleave, so it was noise. `0731` is the first checkpoint where the strict and flexible extractors disagree at all; on every prior baseline they were identical. Perf — pinned llama-benchy standard (fp8 KV, prefix-cache on, `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, mml 49152, util 0.85; C=1, 3 runs), against the **full** recorded range of the prior MTP2 baselines. This crosses a checkpoint boundary, so read it as a sanity band rather than a controlled A/B: | metric | prior MTP2 range (n=10) | 0731 + DSpark | vs band | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | pp2048 @ d8192 | 1339.11 – 1400.81 | **1432.23** ± 11.74 | **above** | | pp2048 @ d16384 | 1308.77 – 1344.68 | **1356.56** ± 11.78 | **above** | | pp2048 @ d32768 | 1089.05 – 1226.63 | **1250.75** ± 2.18 | **above** | | ctx_pp @ d8192 | 1757.16 – 1876.01 | 1816.97 ± 5.89 | inside | | ctx_pp @ d16384 | 1769.85 – 1842.16 | 1817.43 ± 1.43 | inside | | ctx_pp @ d32768 | 1595.87 – 1756.01 | 1740.22 ± 2.87 | inside | | tg128 @ d8192 | 36.27 – 43.08 | 41.72 ± 5.09 | inside | | tg128 @ d16384 | 34.59 – 43.14 | 37.92 ± 9.92 | inside | | tg128 @ d32768 | 32.77 – 42.91 | 34.88 ± 5.78 | inside | | ctx_tg @ d8192 | 38.52 – 43.01 | 39.37 ± 2.34 | inside | | ctx_tg @ d16384 | 39.29 – 43.07 | **35.07** ± 0.67 | **below, −10.7%** | | ctx_tg @ d32768 | 38.02 – 42.73 | 40.70 ± 6.85 | inside | **Batched prefill (pp2048) is above the historical band at all three depths** (+2.2% / +0.9% / +2.0%) — the only consistent directional move here. Clearing the max of ten prior runs at all three depths says more than any single one of those margins would: +0.9% is inside this metric's own resolution, so read the consistency rather than the magnitudes. No sign of DSpark being slower than MTP2 was. One caveat reported rather than buried: **`ctx_tg @ d16384` sits 10.7% below its historical minimum**, the only metric outside its band. It is non-monotonic against our own neighbouring depths (39.37 at d8192, 40.70 at d32768, where history has d16384 ≈ d8192), which points at a single-run artifact rather than a depth-specific regression. **Resolved:** repeated on later heads and it did not recur. A measurement caveat for anyone benchmarking this branch: the `±` in a benchy row is the spread of the three runs *inside one invocation*, and it runs 5–30× smaller than the build-to-build spread. This branch's own history spans 31% on tg128 @ d32768 and ~1.3% on ctx_pp, so anything under ~15% on tg or ~2% on ctx_pp is not resolvable this way. ## Update 2026-08-04 — four fixes from community reports, 35 upstream commits, and first SM120 validation Validated head **`0f59188db1`** (tag `sm120-pr-41834-stable-preview-20260804`). **This is the first head validated on both SM121 and SM120.** Every SM120 discrete-GPU result on this PR up to now was a contributor's measurement we could not reproduce. We have since rebuilt a 2× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell box as a first-party SM120 target. ### Fixes - **DSpark's fused Markov sampler could emit an out-of-vocab token id** (`e171c51036`). `_dspark_markov_probs_blocks_kernel` stores `vocab_size` as the filler for a block with no active lane. On a fully-masked row — every candidate `-inf`, which structured-output constraints can produce — *no* block has an active lane, so every block stores the filler and the reduce kernel returns it verbatim as the sampled token. Nothing downstream bounded it: the runner clamped `input_ids` with `min=0` only, and the DSv4 hash-MoE router indexes `tid2eid[token_id * 6 + lane]` on a `[vocab_size, 6]` table. Result is an illegal memory access on every TP rank. This is the producer on the **V1** path, which is this branch's default. @alexbi29's report traced the same class of defect to the V2 samplers (#50843) — a real defect, but a different tree. Fixed by folding out-of-range to `0` (matching `torch.argmax` on such a row, so the fused kernel stays bit-identical to the eager reference) and making the runner clamp two-sided. Worth stating plainly for anyone with similar gates: **our own gates could not have caught this**. The fused path is skipped when `all_greedy`, and both our long-context recall gate and GSM8K are greedy, so they are structurally incapable of executing that kernel. The new regression test is explicitly non-greedy. - **Adopted #50844** (`3df857ba50`) — bound `token_id` before the `tid2eid` gather. Defence in depth; `prompt_token_ids` reach that gather directly when `--skip-tokenizer-init` disables the engine's vocab check. **Not** taking #50843 (V2-tree only, inert on our default) or #50845, which has a defect reported on its own thread. - **Eager scratch pool is now OFF by default** (`d42b8d9f55`, `b1ef3033f4`), opt-in via `VLLM_DEEPSEEK_V4_EAGER_SCRATCH_POOL=1`. @tobymao bisected output corruption under concurrent mixed prefill+decode to it: pool active 7/7 rounds corrupt, disabled 0/2. We first removed the cross-template aliasing (`max()` → `sum()` sizing with per-family offsets); **they tested that commit directly and it was still corrupt in round 1**. Their diagnosis is the useful part: the pre-pool code was race-free *for free* because per-call transients go through the caching allocator, whose cross-stream reuse is event-guarded — the pool reuses memory without that machinery, so no static partitioning fixes it. Making the cross-layer reuse safe needs producer-waits-on-consumer events against the real stream graph; until then, off by default. - **Two contributor PRs merged** — jasl/vllm#37 (tuned FP8 W8A8 config for `N=4096,K=12288` on RTX PRO 6000) and jasl/vllm#38 (hoist the E8M0 block-scale upcast out of the FP8 GEMM hot path, 13,561 kernel launches removed per 25 decode steps), both from @alexbi29. - **`num_speculative_tokens` rule relaxed.** Upstream removed its own assertion in #50869 as "invalid". They were right that erroring *above* `dspark_block_size` is wrong — two users on this thread run `nst=7` against `block_size=5` and it demonstrably works. The two directions are not symmetric, so this branch now **errors below** the block size (that genuinely garbles output) and **warns above** it, quoting the acceptance cost. Strictly more permissive than what shipped before. ### Validation Full gate battery on **both** architectures, same branch: | gate | SM121 (2× GB10, 2-node TP=2) | SM120 (2× RTX PRO 6000, TP=2) | | --- | --- | --- | | serve, DSpark nst=5, `--block-size 256` | ✅ | ✅ | | instruction-following (jasl/vllm#19) | PASS | PASS | | long-context recall, arthur c=1 | 2/2 | 2/2 | | long-context recall, arthur c=12 | 22, 23, 22 / 24 | 22, 23 / 24 | | GSM8K 8-shot flexible | 0.9484 / 0.9507 / 0.9492 | 0.9371 | | GSM8K 8-shot strict | 0.9462 / 0.9477 / 0.9462 | 0.9303 | | tool-calling, 135 cases | 256/270 (94.8%) | — | | illegal-access / assertion lines | 0 | 0 | The ~1.1 pp GSM8K difference between architectures sits inside this gate's measured single-run spread and spans different silicon, different memory architecture and a 3× smaller KV cache (6.25 GiB vs ~18.5 GiB). We are not claiming a difference from it. **`Check failed: num_tokens > 64` does not reproduce on this branch.** @fuzzifikation reported stock 0.26.0 dying there on SM120 at `--block-size 256`, correctly tracing it to the DSv4 decode dispatch requiring `page_block_size == 64`. On our SM120 box, at the same `--block-size 256`, the serve comes up and the assertion never appears — the DSv4 packed KV cache is laid out in 64-token pages independent of vLLM's logical block size, and FlashInfer derives `page_block_size` from tensor geometry rather than the engine config. The SM120 packed decode path is confirmed engaged in the same run. Note the same assertion has **two** distinct gates (`page_block_size` and `(num_heads, topk)`, the latter being #50720 / flashinfer#3989), so patching one and still seeing it means checking the other. ### Prefill: V1 vs V2 model runner The 2026-08-02 V1-vs-V2 comparison never measured throughput. It has now been measured, blocked and pre-registered — 10 blocks, both arms inside each node pair, exact sign-flip permutation test, Holm-corrected across the six prefill cells, with the decision rule committed before any data was collected: | metric | V2 / V1 | 95% CI | exact p | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | ctx_pp @ d8192 | **+1.18%** | [+0.82, +1.53] | 0.0020 | | ctx_pp @ d16384 | **+1.11%** | [+0.35, +1.87] | 0.0137 | | ctx_pp @ d32768 | **+1.61%** | [+1.17, +2.04] | 0.0020 | | pp2048 @ d8192 | **+4.18%** | [+3.28, +5.09] | 0.0020 | | pp2048 @ d16384 | **+4.18%** | [+3.36, +5.00] | 0.0020 | | pp2048 @ d32768 | **+4.33%** | [+3.56, +5.11] | 0.0020 | All six survive Holm; both node pairs agree in direction on every cell. **Decode is not resolved in either direction** — `tg128` was declared unresolvable before the run (its within-build spread equals its entire historical range) and is reported for the record only. **V1 was the default when this was written; that was reversed on 2026-08-09 — see Update 2026-08-09.** The reasoning below was correct on the evidence available at the time, and the collapse it describes was real; it turned out not to be a property of the runner. Kept unedited because how the conclusion failed is the useful part. V2 is ahead on prefill, KV headroom (+4.70 GiB) and draft acceptance (+6.6%), but its long-context recall under concurrency is unreliable in a way that is worse than a consistent deficit: across 14 independent serves on the same build and configuration, roughly two thirds land in a state that loses most of the needles (arthur c=12 as low as 3/24), while the rest match V1 at 22–24/24. The mode is fixed at startup and stable within a serve, and nothing we have found predicts or detects it. A deployment could run clean for days and restart into the bad mode. The cause is **not identified**. Eliminated so far: the eager-scratch cross-template aliasing, the upstream merges, and the eager scratch pool as a whole (pool on 2 good / 6 bad vs pool off 3 good / 3 bad over 14 serves — no effect). The startup logs of a good and a bad serve are structurally identical, which rules out "a different code path was taken". Anyone opting into V2 with `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1` should know this. ### Measurement note Two errors from our own process, since they affect how the numbers above should be read. The n=8 sampling that originally established V2's recall deficit took eight gate runs from **one serve** — it measured within-serve variance while the quantity that actually varies is across-serve. Raising n on the wrong axis. The 14-serve figures above use the inverted design: many serves, few gates each. And the `±` in a benchy row is the spread *within one invocation*; it runs 5–30× smaller than the build-to-build spread. The blocked design above exists because of that: a coarse range screen over the same 10 blocks returns "no measurable difference" on all six prefill cells, while the paired test finds all six. Had the screen been the decisive statistic, this section would have concluded the opposite and been wrong. ## Update 2026-08-09 — the V2 recall collapse was a prefix-cache race, not the runner; V2 becomes the default 70 upstream commits (to `643c125fab`), and the long-standing reason this branch pinned V1 is gone: it was **an unfixed upstream bug**, not a property of the V2 model runner. ### The defect `FullAttentionManager.cache_blocks()` commits prefix block hashes to the shared `BlockPool` **at scheduling time, before the forward pass writes their KV**. A request admitted later in the same step can match those hashes and read unwritten values. `MambaManager` has guarded this since #29387; no other manager does. This is **vllm-project/vllm#42359**, open and unmerged. Two more reports look like the same triple on different models — **#50188** (prefix caching + MTP spec decode + fp8 KV, byte-identical repeat requests, RTX 5090 / Qwen3.6-27B-NVFP4) and **#43559** (closed without a merged fix). Anyone on `--enable-prefix-caching` with speculative decoding is exposed; DeepSeek-V4 is not special here. What makes it hard to catch: **the damage persists**. A serve that loses the race keeps serving from the poisoned blocks for its lifetime, so a later *serial* request fails too — which is why it looked like a per-serve "mode" rather than a race. It is also stochastic, roughly half of cold serves. ### Evidence Same binary, `VLLM_ALLOW_SPEC_DEC_SAME_STEP_PREFIX_HIT` the only variable, cache populated by the real gate, **4 fresh serves per arm** (a single clean serve proves nothing at ~50% incidence), 3 arthur c=12 runs each: | | serve 1 | serve 2 | serve 3 | serve 4 | mean | min | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | guard **off** | 22/23/24 | **6/5/3** | **14/9/10** | **7/8/7** | 11.5 | 3 | | guard **on** | 23/22/21 | 20/22/20 | 22/23/23 | 23/22/23 | 22.0 | 20 | Mann-Whitney U, p = 0.0043. Every serve's runner and guard state was read back from the serve log rather than assumed. **It also fixes V1**, which was not expected: V1's arthur c=12 goes 20.7 → 23.0 with the guard on (24.0 with prefix caching disabled entirely). V1's own 2–4 needle shortfall was the same defect, not an inherent concurrency margin. ### Runner arbitration, re-run on the fixed tree Same tree, same guard mode, **runner the only variable**: | | V1 | V2 | | --- | --- | --- | | arthur c=12, 4 serves × 3 | 22.3 / 21.7 / 21.7 / 21.0 → **21.67** | 22.0 / 20.7 / 22.7 / 22.7 → **22.00** | | pp2048 d8192 / 16384 / 32768 | 1427 / 1363 / 1216 | **1472 / 1421 / 1303** (+3.1% / +4.2% / +7.1%) | | tg128 mean | 39.95 / 41.16 / 35.25 | **41.56 / 49.61 / 45.18** | | e2e TTFT | 1437 / 1506 / 1689 ms | **1393 / 1444 / 1576 ms** | | GPU KV cache | 339,194 tok | **423,752 tok** (+24.9%) | | GSM8K strict / flexible | 0.9378 / 0.9401 | 0.9401 / 0.9439 | | issue19 · multi-needle · c=1 | PASS · 48/48, 0 leaks · 2/2 | PASS · 48/48, 0 leaks · 2/2 | Recall: p = 0.697, neither side with a single-digit serve. GSM8K differs by <0.4 pp against ~1.1 pp single-run noise. **V2 is not behind anywhere and leads on throughput, latency and KV headroom, so it becomes the default.** `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` still selects V1, which stays supported. **Correction:** the *"V2 +6.6% draft acceptance"* figure in Update 2026-08-04 does **not** survive re-measurement — 2.772 (V1) vs 2.710 (V2) on the same formula and sample size, i.e. a tie. It was measured while V2 was poisoned. ### If you are running this branch **Nothing to set — the guard is on by default where it matters.** `KVCacheCoordinator` enables it whenever prefix caching and speculative decoding are both active, which is the only configuration in which a block hash can be published before its KV is written *and* a second request admitted in the same step to match it. This correction matters: an earlier revision of this update shipped V2 as the default while leaving the guard off by default, which would have handed a plain serve the exact combination measured at mean 11.5 with a 3/24 floor. Both changes looked like improvements in isolation. If you pulled `c054feedac`, take `aa0d513027` instead, or set the variable yourself. To turn it **off** (it is a real escape hatch, pinned by a test): ```bash VLLM_ALLOW_SPEC_DEC_SAME_STEP_PREFIX_HIT=0 ``` `1` is upstream's semantics, gated on `use_eagle`; on DeepSeek-V4 that covers only **2 of 5** managers and leaves the main MLA path unguarded — measured, not assumed, via a startup log line this branch adds that reports how many managers are actually guarded. `2` covers every group and is what the engine selects. Regression sweep on the merged tree: 261 passed, 1 failed, that one failing identically on the pre-merge tree `4ebd1fb698`. ### The two endpoints disagreed about the same model, twice `ResponsesRequest.reasoning` took its type from the OpenAI SDK, whose `ReasoningEffort` stops at `xhigh`, so DeepSeek's documented top tier `max` was rejected by schema validation on `/v1/responses` while `/v1/chat/completions` accepted it. Worse, and on the default path: with no thinking kwarg, `DeepSeekV4Tokenizer.apply_chat_template` defaults thinking **on** while `DeepSeekV4ReasoningParser` defaults it **off** and selects `IdentityReasoningParser`. The model reasoned and its reasoning, with a bare ``, came back inside `output_text` as though it were the answer — whenever a request omitted `reasoning`, which is exactly what a stock OpenAI SDK sends. Chat was immune only because it normalises thinking state at the protocol boundary, and its own docstring says why: *"so the tokenizer and reasoning parser see the same effective state"*. Responses never called that hook. The derivation now lives in `deepseek_v4_chat_kwargs` and both request types call it, so a third endpoint cannot repeat it. Measured on both checkpoints with no workaround flag set, 21/21 each: | | `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` | `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` | | --- | --- | --- | | silence: reasoning in its own field | PASS | PASS | | silence: no `` in the answer | PASS | PASS | | `effort: none` disables thinking | PASS | PASS | | six spellings × two endpoints | PASS | PASS | | `high` reasons deeper than `low` | +85% / +110% | +19% / +35% | 26 unit cases accompany it, 11 of which fail on the unpatched tree. `tests/reasoning` 440 passed, `tests/tokenizers_/test_deepseek_v4.py` 45 passed. ### Acceptance on the exact published SHA Everything above was re-measured on `d44e224ab9` — the commit this tag points at, after a second upstream sync (17 further commits, FlashInfer 0.6.16.post3) — not on an ancestor assumed to be equivalent. 17 of 18 checks pass: | check | result | | --- | --- | | four nodes clean at the SHA, FlashInfer 0.6.16.post3 | PASS | | `tests/v1/core` | 509 passed, 1 pre-existing failure | | default serve with **nothing set**: boots, runner V2, guard 5/5, no NameError | PASS | | arthur c=12 ×3 / c=1 | 22 / 20 / 23 · 2/2 | | GSM8K strict · issue19 · multi-needle | 0.9363 · PASS · 48/48, 0 leaks | | pp2048 d8192 | 1480.77 (arbitration V2 arm 1471.8) | | `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` → V1, guard still 5/5, c=1 2/2 | PASS | | `VLLM_ALLOW_SPEC_DEC_SAME_STEP_PREFIX_HIT=0` → guard 0/5, c=1 2/2 | PASS | **The one non-pass, and what it turned out to be.** `tests/v1/spec_decode` does not complete on this hardware — it wedges under a 30-minute bound on this head and on `4ebd1fb698` alike. Narrowed to `test_max_len.py` and measured both ways: | how it is run | result | | --- | --- | | whole file, one pytest process | wedges after ~7 min, 5 of 11 done | | each case in its own process | **11 of 11 pass**, free memory steady at 117 GiB | No individual case is broken. Each stands up a full engine, and repeated create/tear-down inside one process does not release resources fast enough on a **single-GPU** unified-memory node. That also explains why both trees wedge and why they stop at different points. It remains **unverified coverage rather than a pass**; running one process per case produces a verdict instead of a hang. `test_async_scheduling_pp_allows_rescheduling_with_output_placeholders` is the same class: it builds `pipeline_parallel_size=2`, and a GB10 node has one GPU, so it fails at config construction. It is the only case in `tests/v1/core` that needs more than one GPU; the other 509 pass. ### What this arbitration does and does not cover Everything above was measured on **one configuration**: 2-node TP=2, `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`, DSpark `num_speculative_tokens: 5`, fp8 KV, `max_model_len` 131072, prefix caching on, GB10 (SM121). The default now applies to **every** DSpark config, including shapes not measured here — TP=4, other context lengths, the NVFP4 checkpoint, single-node setups. The reasoning generalises better than the numbers do: the race is in block publication and is not specific to a model shape, and V2's advantage comes from KV headroom and scheduling rather than anything config-specific. But if you run a materially different shape and see something worse, `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` returns you to V1 and a report would be welcome — that is a gap in our coverage, not a claim we have ruled out. ## Running DSpark DSpark is DeepSeek's self-drafting speculative-decode variant; on `0731` the draft weights are carried in the main checkpoint, so no separate `--speculative-model` is needed. ```bash vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 \ --trust-remote-code \ --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 \ --tool-call-parser deepseek_v4 --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4 \ --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --block-size 256 \ --max-model-len 49152 \ --max-num-seqs 64 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' ``` - `num_speculative_tokens` **must equal** the checkpoint's `dspark_block_size` (5). Larger values are rejected: they are never accepted and only waste draft compute. - `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` is mandatory — DSv4's `fp8_ds_mla` attention asserts an fp8 KV layout, so the default `auto` fails at model construction. Not DSpark-specific. - Runs on the **V1 runner by default** (correct long-context recall). `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1` opts into the V2 DSpark speculator; V2's long-context recall is correct after the jasl/vllm#26 padded-Q fix. - If you measure draft acceptance yourself, **use prose**. On counting or repeated text the Markov head alone reaches 68–100% acceptance even with the neural draft path degraded, which hides real regressions entirely. ## Dependencies (stock-deps path) Pins on the current head: torch 2.13.0 (triton 3.7.1) · `flashinfer-python` / `flashinfer-cubin` 0.6.15.post1 · tilelang 0.1.12 · `nvidia-cutlass-dsl[cu13]` 4.6.0 · `quack-kernels>=0.6.1` · nvidia-nccl-cu13 2.30.7 (multi-node, see below). - **FlashInfer** is pinned in `requirements/cuda.txt` (`flashinfer-python` **and** the GitHub-release `flashinfer-cubin`, which must be the same version); it ships the SM120 packed sparse-MLA kernels, so a stock build picks them up with no manual install dance. - **GB10 / multi-node**: pin `nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.30.7` on every node. A rebuild silently reverts it to torch's bundled version, and a per-node mismatch hangs the NCCL handshake. - The SM120 **decode** (`VLLM_DEEPSEEK_V4_FLASHINFER_SM120_DECODE`) and **prefill** (`VLLM_DEEPSEEK_V4_FLASHINFER_SM120_PREFILL`) FlashInfer sparse-MLA paths **default on**; set either `=0` to fall back to the FlashMLA / Triton path. Both are availability-gated, so stock installs without the kernel degrade gracefully rather than raising. ## Running the NVFP4 checkpoint This branch also serves `nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-NVFP4` on SM12x (RTX PRO 6000 / GB10). The NVFP4 MoE auto-selects the FlashInfer CUTLASS backend (the SwiGLU-clamp model gate accepts it), so no `--moe-backend` flag and no special FlashInfer build are required: ```bash vllm serve nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-NVFP4 \ --trust-remote-code --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 ``` Expert-parallel off (plain TP) is the supported path. Accuracy matches MXFP4 (GSM8K 8-shot ~0.96 on both SM120 and SM121). On SM12x NVFP4 is **not** a memory or throughput win versus MXFP4: NVFP4 weights are ~4 GiB/GPU larger, leaving less KV-cache room; single-stream prefill is marginally faster and aggregate decode marginally slower. Its value here is checkpoint availability / parity with the SM100 datacenter path — MXFP4 remains the better practical choice on consumer Blackwell. ## AI assistance disclosure AI assistants, including OpenAI Codex/GPT models and Anthropic Claude models, were used for code review, refactoring support, regression-script writing, and benchmark analysis. The branch was validated through human review plus the commands and harness artifacts listed above; every performance and accuracy number quoted was measured on real SM120/SM121 hardware.

This admits SM110 as well as SM120/121. The MARLIN-first ordering and kernel constraints added for SM12x are gated on capability family 120, so Thor does not receive them. Restoring the SM11x exclusion while retaining SM12x support fixes the tested Thor configuration. The validated change replaces the CUDA return condition with: ```python if cap is None: return False cap_tuple = (cap.major, cap.minor) return (9, 0) <= cap_tuple < (11, 0) or (12, 0) <= cap_tuple < (13, 0) ``` Applied to the failing nightly on the same pinned base image, this restores automatic MARLIN selection, removes the compilation failure, and completes the GSM8K evaluation without a `--moe-backend` override. GSM8K figures above are flexible-extract exact match, five-shot, on a 10% subset, using the evaluation options `--tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --limit 0.1` with the `openai-completions` backend. Each figure is from one run. This validates startup and evaluation completion for `gpt-oss-120b` MXFP4 on Thor at TP=1; it does not establish full-dataset accuracy equivalence or performance. Other GPU architectures and `gpt-oss-20b` were not exercised in this validation. #### Release relevance Source inspection on October 13, 2026 found the widened gate in both [`v0.31.1rc0`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.31.1rc0/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/experts/gpt_oss_triton_kernels_moe.py) and [`v0.32.0rc0`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.32.0rc0/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/experts/gpt_oss_triton_kernels_moe.py). Those tags were checked at source level, not separately run on hardware. [`v0.31.0`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/v0.31.0/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/experts/gpt_oss_triton_kernels_moe.py) retains the SM110 exclusion and predates this regression. Could the SM110 safeguard be restored while preserving the SM12x support from #58877, and the fix considered for the upcoming releases? cc @wtdcode @mgoin *Drafted with AI assistance — Codex.* ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

## Overview

#41834 has been stale for a while, and many key contributions have been superseded by other PRs. This PR extracts the useful parts of that huge PR and conducts end-to-end experiments on two Sparks to ensure it works well. The authorship is also acknowledged.

## Claims

In general, this PR comprises:

- **mHC residual reuse.** For a `8192` token prefill setup, this saves 256 MiB VRAM.

issue.title: proposal: fmt: ErrorAppender interface

milestone.title: Proposal
milestone.description:
Proposals that are pending (not yet accepted/rejected).
See https://go.dev/s/proposal-process.

issue.body:
### Proposal Details

## Motivation
It is all too common to find error types in the standard library and in the wild which:
 - Allocate the result of `Error() string` method every time called. i.e: `fmt.Errorf`. 
 - Are defined in a list where a prefix is appended to every defined value i.e: http errors like `ErrHijacked = errors.New("http: connection has been hijacked")` and `ErrUseLastResponse = errors.New("net/http: use last response")`, which demonstrates a another problem:
- Inconsistency in prefix leading the main error message, not 100% relevant to proposal, but worth pointing out


<details><summary>LLM investigated and found many occurences in the Go standard library</summary>

## 1. Alloc on Error
net.OpError, net.ParseError, net.AddrError, net.UnknownNetworkError, net.DNSError, net.DNSConfigError

os.SyscallError, os.PathError, os.LinkError 

url.Error, url.EscapeError, url.InvalidHostError

xml.SyntaxError

The list goes on...

## 2. Package-prefixed sentinel error definitions
Here are some standard-library examples of the convention you're describing.

database/sql
This is a particularly good example. Its exported sentinel errors use the sql: prefix.

Source: [database/sql/sql.go ](https://go.dev/src/database/sql/sql.go?utm_source=chatgpt.com).


```go
var ErrNoRows = errors.New("sql: no rows in result set")

var ErrConnDone = errors.New("sql: connection is already closed")

var ErrTxDone = errors.New(
    "sql: transaction has already been committed or rolled back",
)
```
All three use the package name followed by a colon. 

The HTTP package also uses this convention extensively.
Examples include:


```go
ErrHijacked = errors.New(
    "http: connection has been hijacked",
)
ErrContentLength = errors.New(
    "http: wrote more than the declared Content-Length",
)
ErrBodyReadAfterClose = errors.New(
    "http: invalid Read on closed Body",
)
```
Source: [net/http/server.go ](https://go.dev/src/net/http/server.go?utm_source=chatgpt.com) and [net/http package documentation ](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http?utm_source=chatgpt.com). 

One qualification: net/http isn't completely consistent. Some of its errors use net/http: instead of http:.
The TLS package provides another example of package-qualified error messages, although its alert errors are represented by a type rather than a collection of errors.New sentinel values.

For example, AlertError.Error() delegates to the alert string representation, which uses:

```go
return "tls: " + s
```

</details>


## Proposal
In the spirit of other Append* methods like [encoding.TextAppender (link to Go issue tracker)](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/62384) I propose we add the `fmt.ErrorAppender` interface which is a union of `error` interface and the `ErrorAppend` method:

```go
package fmt

type ErrorAppender interface {
    error
    // ErrorAppend appends the message that would be returned by [error.Error] to dst and returns the result.
    ErrorAppend(dst []byte) []byte
}
```

## Edit: Examples of users
I develop Go on constrained systems and would appreciate controlling the allocations in my program, so I would implement `ErrorAppender` for the errors in my packages. I can also use `fmt.Appendf` (method that would presumably check for `ErrorAppender` implementation on `error`) to build messages to then join errors without allocating given the underlying buffer I've allocated has enough capacity.

Users of my package can also check for ErrorAppender implementation on returned errors and print them without allocating. The errors can be wrapped indefinetely with something like `errors.Prefix` below and still not allocate and not lose expressiveness.

Summarized: the benefits to users are:
- Constrained allocations while not losing expressiveness of errors
- A new Go pattern for standardizing how we define errors which leads to less stutter and consistency across error string return value (with below `errors.Prefix` type)

`Error() string` values in Go almost exclusively follow th pattern `toplevel: wrapped1: wrapped2: ...` which would benefit tremendously from this proposal since we'd go from `N` allocations, N being wrap level, to no allocations if buffer is large enough.

## Example of potential standard library user: `errors.Prefix`
Also, not strictly necessary for this proposal, but I suggest the following `errors` package type:

```go
package errors

// Can be defined at package level and then used to create all package errors with no stutter.
type Prefix struct {
	Prefix string
}

type prefixed struct { // implements the fmt.ErrorAppender interface.
	prefix string
	err    error // edit: was proposed as `string` initially, if error type instead we win Unwrap() functionality, thanks @apparentlymart
}

func (prefix Prefix) NewError(err error) error {
	return &prefixed{prefix: prefix.Prefix, err: err}
}

func (p prefixed) Error() string { return string(p.ErrorAppend(nil)) } // trivial to implement error once ErrorAppend implemented.

func (p prefixed) ErrorAppend(dst []byte) []byte {
	dst = append(dst, p.prefix...)
	if a, ok := p.err.(fmt.ErrorAppender); ok {
		return a.ErrorAppend(dst)
	}
	return append(dst, p.err.Error()...)
}

// use by external third party package:
package mypkg

import "errors"

var pkgerr = errors.Prefix{Prefix: "mypkg: "}

// package errors.
var (
    ErrNoData = pkgerr.NewError("no data") // will format as "mypkg: no data"
    ErrTooMuchData = pkgerr.NewError("too much data") // will format as "mypkg: too much data"
)
```

comment.body: If `ErrorAppend` is useful for error values, then `StringAppend` is useful for types with a `String` method.

proposal: os/signal: new error type to communicate the signal triggered context cancellation

milestone.title: Proposal
milestone.description:
Proposals that are pending (not yet accepted/rejected).
See https://go.dev/s/proposal-process.

issue.body:
<!--
Our proposal process is documented here:
https://go.dev/s/proposal-process
-->

This comes from the need to fix #60733.

In order to provide the information of which signal triggered context cancellation in `signal.NotifyContext` using `context.Cause`, we need a new error type (as that's the only type allowed by context cause) to communicate that info back to the user.

The proposal is to define it as a simple struct that can only be used by pointer as an error:

```go
// CanceledBySignalError represents the error can be retrieved via context.Cause
// on the context returned by NotifyContext to inspect which signal caused the
// cancellation.
type CanceledBySignalError struct {
	// The signal caused the context cancellation.
	Signal os.Signal
}

func (cse *CanceledBySignalError) Error() string {
	return fmt.Sprintf("context canceled by signal %v", cse.Signal)
}
```

So users can inspect the signal via code like:

```go
select {
case <-ctx.Done():
  cause := context.Cause(ctx)
  var cse *signal.CanceledBySignalError
  if errors.As(cause, &cse) {
    sig := cse.Signal
    // Do something with sig
  }
}
```

comment.body:
`fmt.Appendf` takes a format string and a list of arguments. I don't understand how it could use the proposed `ErrorAppend` method.

I understand how `fmt.Append` could use it.

But I'm not personally convinced that this is an important enough issue to merit a magic method. In particular, if we care about `fmt.Append`, I can easily see how a `StringAppend` method could help in some cases, and it seems that it would help in a lot more cases than `ErrorAppend`. But I doubt that people use `fmt.Append` all that often.

issue.title: runtime: statically linked c-archive crashes in sysargs with musl

labels.name: compiler/runtime
labels.description: Issues related to the Go compiler and/or runtime.

issue.body:
### Go version

go1.26.0 linux/amd64

### Environment

Ubuntu 20.04 x86_64, musl-gcc, CGO_ENABLED=1.

### What did you do?

Built a minimal c-archive:

```go
package main

import "C"

//export InitDialer
func InitDialer() C.int { return 0 }

func main() {}
```

Linked it into a minimal static musl executable:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
extern int InitDialer(void);
int main(void) {
    int result = InitDialer();
    printf("InitDialer=%d\n", result);
    return result;
}
```

```sh
CGO_ENABLED=1 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 CC=musl-gcc \
  go build -buildmode=c-archive -o libprobe.a .
musl-gcc -static -g -O0 probe.c libprobe.a \
  -o probe -lpthread -ldl -lm -lresolv
./probe
```

### What did you expect?

The process prints `InitDialer=0` and exits successfully.

### What did you see?

It receives SIGSEGV before reaching `main`:

```text
Thread 2 received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
0x000000000044ae1c in runtime.sysargs ()
#0 runtime.sysargs ()
#1 runtime.args ()
#2 runtime.args.abi0 ()
#3 runtime.rt0_go.abi0 ()
```

A breakpoint on `_rt0_amd64_lib` shows `rsi=0` and an unrelated nonzero `rdi`, so `sysargs` walks an invalid argv/environment layout.

Disassembly of musl `__libc_start_init` shows that it invokes `.init_array` entries with `callq *(%rbx)` without passing argc/argv. In contrast, `_rt0_amd64_lib` expects argc/argv in the C ABI registers. The same archive works when linked with glibc.

I verified that changing the musl c-archive entry to use `argc=0` and `argv=environ-1` lets Go skip the environment and locate auxv, and the probe then returns successfully. This is only a diagnostic workaround: a complete fix should also preserve `os.Args` semantics rather than unconditionally setting argc to zero.

issue.body:
I know there was a proposal about decimal as an std package.
But according to https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_floating_point, there have already been multiple compliant hardware implementations, and supported by several commonly used programming languages. I think having decimal as first-class citizen like the other part of the IEEE-754 standard makes sense.

The upside is we don't have to spend the effort on API design upfront to make it useful like math.big. We can just limit the scope of the operations only within the Go's existing arithmetic operators. Designing a good numerical/arithmetic API beyond the conventional operators is harder and can be deferred later with no harm.

comment.body:
@marcelocantos 

I don't have a clear opinion on whether we should a builtin type or a library. That said, I want to make a couple of points.

> The libraries that need updating are those whose users ask for decimal support or which are intended to cover types exhaustively.

In general libraries that use reflection are general purpose libraries that are indeed intended to cover types exhaustively. This is not a special case, it is the normal case. We can't casually dismiss this issue.

> Reflection sees it as a struct with unexported fields, so an encoder without hand-written support emits `{}` and carries on.

We have standardized ways to handle encoders in the standard library encoding package (https://pkg.go.dev/encoding). All plausible encoders use those interfaces, so this is not a significant issue.

issue.title: strings: speed up ASCII ToUpper and ToLower by writing directly into a buffer instead of using Builder
issue.body:
https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/go/+/858401

### Summary

- The ASCII paths of [strings.ToUpper](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2b74366d84da17ba4de6cecf1219386647f20d6f/src/strings/strings.go#L679-L703) and [strings.ToLower](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2b74366d84da17ba4de6cecf1219386647f20d6f/src/strings/strings.go#L719-L743) use strings.Builder. [bytes.ToUpper](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2b74366d84da17ba4de6cecf1219386647f20d6f/src/bytes/bytes.go#L691-L705) and [bytes.ToLower](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2b74366d84da17ba4de6cecf1219386647f20d6f/src/bytes/bytes.go#L722-L735) use bytealg.MakeNoZero instead.
- When the result length is known, bytealg.MakeNoZero is better than strings.Builder. Builder runs copyCheck and a capacity check on every write, and calls memmove for each run. With a buffer allocated once by MakeNoZero, the loop just writes by index, and the compiler also eliminates the bounds check inside the loop.

### Change

Make the ASCII path of the `strings` version match the `bytes` version. Returning `s` unchanged when no conversion is needed, and the number of allocations (one), stay the same.

`ToUpper` (`ToLower` gets the same change, and `strings.go` gains an `unsafe` import):

```diff
@@ -681,24 +682,13 @@ func ToUpper(s string) string {
 			return s
 		}
-		var (
-			b   Builder
-			pos int
-		)
-		b.Grow(len(s))
+		b := bytealg.MakeNoZero(len(s))[:len(s):len(s)]
 		for i := 0; i < len(s); i++ {
 			c := s[i]
 			if 'a' <= c && c <= 'z' {
 				c -= 'a' - 'A'
-				if pos < i {
-					b.WriteString(s[pos:i])
-				}
-				b.WriteByte(c)
-				pos = i + 1
 			}
+			b[i] = c
 		}
-		if pos < len(s) {
-			b.WriteString(s[pos:])
-		}
-		return b.String()
+		return unsafe.String(unsafe.SliceData(b), len(b))
 	}
 	return Map(unicode.ToUpper, s)
```

### Benchmarks

`go version go1.28-devel_2b74366d84 Tue Nov 3 05:37:40 2026 -0800 darwin/arm64` (built from master at 2b74366d84), Apple M4 Max (darwin/arm64), `-count 10`, compared with benchstat.

| Benchmark | Old | New | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| ToUpper/abc | 16.79n | 10.42n | -37.89% |
| ToUpper/AbC123 | 20.85n | 12.20n | -41.52% |
| ToUpper/longStrinGwitHmixofsmaLLandcAps | 76.24n | 26.05n | -65.83% |
| ToUpper/RENAN_BASTOS_93_AOSDAJDJAIDJAIDAJIaidsjjaidijadsjiadjiOOKKO | 94.65n | 56.82n | -39.96% |
| ToLower/AbC123 | 21.09n | 11.46n | -45.66% |
| ToLower/longStrinGwitHmixofsmaLLandcAps | 57.59n | 26.43n | -54.10% |
| ToLower/renan_bastos_93_AOSDAJDJAIDJAIDAJIaidsjjaidijadsjiadjiOOKKO | 87.34n | 49.34n | -43.51% |
| geomean | 25.94n | 18.99n | -26.79% |

issue.title: mime: ParseMediaType allocates repeatedly for quoted parameters

labels.name: NeedsInvestigation
labels.description: Someone must examine and confirm this is a valid issue and not a duplicate of an existing one.

issue.body:
### Go version

```text
go version go1.28-devel_babb75be Sun Nov 1 14:19:14 2026 -0800 darwin/arm64
```

The baseline source revision is
babb75be8cd5a3b1cd1a34fd837225cbef659d10. Baseline and candidate benchmark
binaries use this same toolchain and the same test sources; the baseline
implementation of mediatype.go is selected through a build overlay.

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace

```text
darwin/arm64: GOARM64=v8.0 CGO_ENABLED=1
linux/amd64:  GOAMD64=v1   CGO_ENABLED=0
```

The arm64 host is an Apple M4 Pro running macOS 27.0.1. The amd64 binaries
were cross-compiled with the same toolchain, then executed natively on
an Intel Xeon Gold 6238R in a shared, 16-vCPU KVM guest. The Linux process
was pinned to CPU 15 with nice level 10. The guest was not exclusive;
its timing samples are noisier than the arm64 samples.

### What did you do?

Parsed an ordinary Content-Disposition value with a quoted filename:

```go
mediaType, params, err := mime.ParseMediaType(
    `attachment; filename="report.pdf"`,
)
// mediaType == "attachment", params["filename"] == "report.pdf", err == nil
```

A multipart upload also uses this path, for example:

```http
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="report.pdf"
```

In the standard library, multipart.Part.FileName calls
parseContentDisposition, which calls mime.ParseMediaType:
https://github.com/golang/go/blob/babb75be8cd5a3b1cd1a34fd837225cbef659d10/src/mime/multipart/multipart.go#L88

A standalone benchmark of the public API is:

```go
package mime_test

import (
    "mime"
    "testing"
)

var (
    mediaTypeResult string
    parametersResult map[string]string
    parseErrorResult error
)

func BenchmarkParseMediaTypeFilename(b *testing.B) {
    for b.Loop() {
        mediaTypeResult, parametersResult, parseErrorResult =
            mime.ParseMediaType(`attachment; filename="report.pdf"`)
    }
}
```

Run it with a toolchain built from the baseline source:

```sh
go test -run='^$' -bench=BenchmarkParseMediaTypeFilename -benchmem
```

### What did you see happen?

consumeValue builds each quoted value byte by byte in a strings.Builder,
even when the value needs no unescaping. The builder can grow repeatedly
for one parameter. The returned media type and parameters are correct;
the issue is avoidable allocation and copying.

For `attachment; filename="report.pdf"`, the public API takes four
allocations and 360 B/op on both platforms. Two allocations are for the
quoted value itself. A synthetic 900-byte filename requires eleven
allocations in the public API, nine of them for the quoted value.

### What did you expect to see?

A quoted value that needs no unescaping can be scanned before allocating
its result. Its storage can then be allocated once at the required size.
For malformed input, the scan can fail before building a partial value.

The optimization should preserve the existing parsing rules, including
literal backslashes in legacy Windows paths, escaped separators, CR/LF
rejection, and byte handling for non-ASCII or invalid UTF-8 input. It
should also preserve separate storage for a decoded quoted value, so
retaining a short name does not newly retain the complete header string.

A local implementation keeps the existing
escape-handling loop for values that require decoding. No API change is
proposed.

Selected results from `BenchmarkParseMediaTypeQuoted` are below. Each
platform used 12 alternating baseline/candidate pairs, 200ms per case,
`GOMAXPROCS=1`, and `-test.cpu=1`. Times are benchstat medians. The
LongFilename case is synthetic, not a claim about typical header size.

| Case | arm64 ns/op, before → after | Change | amd64 ns/op, before → after | Change | allocs/op, before → after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Filename | 155.2 → 140.3 | -9.54%, p<0.001 | 843.5 → 665.5 | -21.11%, p=0.002 | 4 → 3 |
| FormData | 210.8 → 190.8 | -9.46%, p<0.001 | 1035.5 → 867.9 | -16.19%, p=0.010 | 5 → 4 |
| LongFilename | 2213.5 → 934.1 | -57.80%, p<0.001 | 7346 → 3031 | -58.74%, p<0.001 | 11 → 3 |

The existing aggregate `BenchmarkParseMediaType` decreases from 444 to
402 allocs/op, but its timing change is not statistically significant
on either platform (arm64 p=0.128; amd64 p=0.198).

There are small helper-level regressions. For an empty quoted value,
`consumeValue` rises from 2.063 to 2.277 ns on arm64 (+10.37%) and from
7.325 to 8.309 ns on amd64 (+13.43%). On arm64, escapes at prefix lengths
0 and 1 rise by 1.36 and 1.22 ns (+6.79% and +5.62%). These cases have
unchanged allocations. Public API cases for empty values and these
early escapes show no statistically significant timing difference in
these runs. The noisy amd64 measurements do not establish equivalence.

The candidate passes the MIME package tests on both native platforms.
Local allocation checks fail as expected against the baseline and pass
against the candidate. A 30-second differential fuzz run on arm64
completed 11,378,351 executions against the baseline parser without a
mismatch. These allocation and differential checks are local research
checks; the compact patch adds boundary cases and public API benchmarks.
The full all.bash suite also passes on darwin/arm64 with only the compact
patch.
The full Linux suite was not run.

The measurements concern ParseMediaType; end-to-end HTTP throughput and
latency have not been measured.

issue.title: proposal: net: Disable MPTCP by default

milestone.title: Proposal
milestone.description:
Proposals that are pending (not yet accepted/rejected).
See https://go.dev/s/proposal-process.

issue.body:
### Proposal Details

See https://www.anthropic.com/research/discovering-vulnerabilities-with-claude
Linux MPTCP listener can be attacked, and go listener listen MPTCP by default in https://github.com/golang/go/commit/3d4daa38a763260e07f4745110f2b5fcbec25126
This may expose all golang programs to this vulnerability

NOTE: It is currently **unknown** whether this vulnerability is strongly related to MPTCP

comment.body:
If we believe the advantages of MPTCP, then it seems to clearly make sense to enable it by default. It improves network transmission when it is available, and it falls back seamlessly when it is not.

In general before this security issue I believe that the only complaint has been #74643, which was closed with no action taken.

I'm not in any way wedded to MPTCP. But I don't see any reason that a security issue should lead us to disable it. This is especially true given that the security issue at least potentially affects regular TCP, and it has already been patched, and there is any easy way to avoid it without waiting for the patch.

issue.body:
I know there was a proposal about decimal as an std package.
But according to https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_floating_point, there have already been multiple compliant hardware implementations, and supported by several commonly used programming languages. I think having decimal as first-class citizen like the other part of the IEEE-754 standard makes sense.

The upside is we don't have to spend the effort on API design upfront to make it useful like math.big. We can just limit the scope of the operations only within the Go's existing arithmetic operators. Designing a good numerical/arithmetic API beyond the conventional operators is harder and can be deferred later with no harm.

comment.body:
Thanks for the note.

While it's true that a constant like `2i` is a complex constant, I don't think of the `i` as a suffix. I think of it as the mathematical symbol `i` (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_unit). It's routine in math to write something like `2i` to mean `2` multiplied by the value `i`, so that reads naturally in Go. GCC and clang also support this syntax in C (https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Complex.html), and C++ supports it in general.

As far as I can recall we don't use suffixes for constants in any other way. So it's not obvious to me that a suffix of `g` is the right way to denote a decimal constant.

That said, I'll note that C23 does define suffixes for decimal constants. This is consistent with how C uses numeric suffixes in other ways, such as the suffixes `l` (long) or `u` (unsigned). In C23 the suffixes for decimal floating point are `df`, `dd`, and `dl`. It doesn't seem helpful for Go to choose different, unrelated, suffixes.

Yet there are a great many analyzers that users could and would write, either to enforce internal invariants of their own codebase ("housekeeping") or to help clients of their public packages use the APIs correctly, analogous to how the printf analyzer checks calls to fmt.Printf. issue.title: net: IPMask and HardwareAddr UnmarshalText reject base64 containing newlines that Go 1.27 accepted
issue.body:
### Go version

go version go1.28-devel (tip at 6c49ac31) linux/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/package

(not relevant)

### What did you do?

Go 1.28 adds `UnmarshalText` methods to `net.IPMask` and `net.HardwareAddr` (#29678).
To keep reading JSON written by older Go versions, they fall back to decoding the
old base64 form using a hand-written decoder in package net (`base64Decode` in
`src/net/ip.go`), since net cannot import encoding/base64.

Before Go 1.28 these types were decoded as plain `[]byte`, which uses
`base64.StdEncoding`. That decoder ignores `'\r'` and `'\n'` characters, so
base64 values with line breaks (for example, from producers that wrap base64
output) were accepted. The new decoder in net rejects them.

```go
package main

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"net"
)

func main() {
	// "////AA==" is the base64 encoding of the mask 255.255.255.0,
	// as produced by json.Marshal in Go 1.27 and earlier.
	for _, in := range []string{`"////AA=="`, `"////\nAA=="`, `"////AA==\r\n"`} {
		var m net.IPMask
		err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(in), &m)
		var h net.HardwareAddr
		err2 := json.Unmarshal([]byte(in), &h)
		var b []byte
		err3 := json.Unmarshal([]byte(in), &b)
		fmt.Printf("%-16s IPMask=%v err=%v | HardwareAddr=%v err=%v | []byte=%x err=%v\n", in, m, err, h, err2, b, err3)
	}
}
```

### What did you see happen?

Go 1.27.3: all three inputs decode to `ffffff00`.

Tip: the inputs containing `\n` or `\r\n` fail with
`invalid IP address` / `invalid MAC address`, while decoding the same
input into a `[]byte` still succeeds.

I found this by differential testing: decoding about 20,000 randomly
mutated base64 strings into `IPMask` and `HardwareAddr` with Go 1.27.3 and with
tip. Apart from the intended new acceptance of IP/MAC text forms, the only
differences were inputs containing `'\r'` or `'\n'`.

### What did you expect to see?

Since the goal is for Go 1.28 and later to read data produced by earlier
versions, I expected the base64 fallback to accept the same inputs as
`base64.StdEncoding` did, by skipping `'\r'` and `'\n'` in `base64Decode`.

This is an edge case: Go's own encoder never emits line breaks. If it is
not worth handling, it may be worth a note in the documentation instead.
I am happy to send a CL for whichever is preferred.

comment.body: I don't see why this is worth handling and I don't see why it's worth documenting. It's important that we handle arbitrary text reasonably. It's not important that we handle it precisely identically. The only text that must be handled identically is text that may be generated by either the old or the new marshaller.

comment.body:
I appreciate the fact that this is being represented as a Go file. But when I read it I can't help but notice a set of restrictions:

- The file must be named goanalysis.go.
- The file must contain the line `//go:build goanalysis`.
- The file must have one or more imports (or it is useless).
- Each import is expected to be annotated with one or more `//go:analyze` comments.
- The import comments restate the import path.
- Any other code in the file is useless in practice.

It feels like there is a certain amount of syntactic ceremony that boils down to exactly the `//go:analyze` comments. And those comments are even Go code anyhow.

Basically we want a mapping from a local import path to a set of (path spec, function) pairs. Should we consider possibilities other than shoehorning that into Go syntax? Such as the go.mod file.

I note in particular the the go.mod file seems particularly appropriate for the "importers" `//go:analyze` form, since the go.mod file is already all about importers.

On the downside the go.mod file does not currently describe subdirectories of the module.

issue.title: os/user: Lookup can return an environment-derived current UID instead of an existing username's passwd entry

labels.name: NeedsInvestigation
labels.description: Someone must examine and confirm this is a valid issue and not a duplicate of an existing one.

issue.body:
### Go version

go1.27.1 and go1.27.3, linux/amd64. Reproduced with `CGO_ENABLED=0` (also with `-tags osusergo`). A cgo build against glibc 2.39 resolves the real account.

### What happens

Given a readable `/etc/passwd`:

```
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh
kubelet:x:1001:1001:kubelet:/var/lib/kubelet:/sbin/nologin
```

a fresh process runs as UID/GID 2001, with `USER=kubelet` and `HOME=/`. UID 2001 has no passwd entry; the name `kubelet` has a real entry at UID 1001.

Pure-Go results:

```
Lookup("kubelet").Uid = "2001"
LookupId("1001").Uid  = "1001"
LookupId("2001").Uid  = "2001"
Current().Uid         = "2001"
```

`LookupId("1001")` reads the real record, so the file is readable and the entry is present. Only the lookup by name returns UID 2001, which belongs to that name only through the environment. The cgo build resolves `Lookup("kubelet")` to UID 1001; there `Current()` and `LookupId("2001")` return unknown-user errors.

### What I expected

`Lookup("kubelet")` returns the passwd record for `kubelet` (UID 1001), not a different UID derived from the environment.

### Why it happens

`Lookup` consults `Current()` before reading the account source (src/os/user/lookup.go):

```go
func Lookup(username string) (*User, error) {
	if u, err := Current(); err == nil && u.Username == username {
		return u, err
	}
	...
}
```

When the process UID has no passwd entry, the pure-Go `current()` builds a `User` from the process IDs and `USER`/`HOME` (src/os/user/lookup_stubs.go). Its `Username` is `$USER`, so a `Lookup` of that same name returns the synthetic result and the named-account lookup never runs. `LookupId` behaves the same way when `Current().Uid` equals the requested id.

### Question

`Current()` deliberately supports processes whose UID has no account record (#14626, #38599). #27524 already made `Current()` prefer the passwd record when the current UID has one (CL 134218); this is the remaining case, where the UID has no entry, so `Current()` is still built from `$USER`, and `Lookup` of that name returns it instead of the name's real record. Should the synthetic result take precedence over an existing record when the caller asks for a specific name or id? If the behavior must stay for compatibility, documenting the provenance and the existence-check limitation on `Lookup`/`LookupId` would help callers.

### Downstream motivation

Kubernetes PR [#141971](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141971) treats a nil `Lookup` error as evidence that an account exists. This is not a privilege-escalation report: the synthetic UID is the process's own UID, and that caller discards the returned UID.

### Reproducer (standard library only)

`main.go`:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"os/user"
	"strconv"
)

func show(label string, u *user.User, err error) {
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Printf("%-18s err: %v\n", label, err)
		return
	}
	fmt.Printf("%-18s Uid=%s Username=%s HomeDir=%s\n", label, u.Uid, u.Username, u.HomeDir)
}

func main() {
	fmt.Printf("uid=%d USER=%q HOME=%q\n", os.Getuid(), os.Getenv("USER"), os.Getenv("HOME"))
	u, e := user.Lookup("kubelet")
	show(`Lookup("kubelet")`, u, e)
	u, e = user.LookupId("1001")
	show(`LookupId("1001")`, u, e)
	u, e = user.LookupId(strconv.Itoa(os.Getuid()))
	show(`LookupId(self)`, u, e)
	cu, ce := user.Current()
	show("Current()", cu, ce)
}
```

Recipe (needs root for the mount namespace and `setpriv`):

```sh
cat > /tmp/fake-passwd <<'EOF'
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh
kubelet:x:1001:1001:kubelet:/var/lib/kubelet:/sbin/nologin
EOF

CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /tmp/repro .

sudo unshare --mount sh -c '
  mount --bind /tmp/fake-passwd /etc/passwd
  setpriv --reuid=2001 --regid=2001 --clear-groups \
    env USER=kubelet HOME=/ /tmp/repro
'
```

For the cgo control, build with `CGO_ENABLED=1` and run the same recipe.

comment.body: Personally I think we should simply document the current behavior. The combination of setting the `USER` environment variable to an entry that exists in /etc/passwd while using a user ID that is not in /etc/passwd seems to me to be a peculiar case. Unless there is some reason to believe that this is common, I think we should just document it.

issue.title: [js-api] Use arithmetic NaN for the NaN case of ToWebAssemblyValue
issue.body:
`ToWebAssemblyValue` converts a JavaScript NaN to f32 (and f64) like this:

```
1. If number is NaN,
    1. Let n be an implementation-defined integer such that canon_32 ≤ n < 2^signif(32).
    1. Let f32 be nan(n).
...
1. Return f32.const f32.
```

The second step has an issue:
(setting aside that `n` should be `|n|` in the original text,)
[core specification for Floating-Point](https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/syntax/values.html#syntax-float) states that `nan(n)` itself is a floating-point magnitude,
and in order to make it a floating-point value, an explicit sign is required,
so current `f32` is not something `f32.const` later can take.

Fixing this in place means choosing a sign in an implementation-defined manner as well:

```
1. Let n be an implementation-defined integer such that canon_32 ≤ n < 2^signif(32).
1. Let f32 be either +nan(n) or −nan(n), chosen in an implementation-defined way.
```

This is a bit wordy though, unnecesariliy spreading the implementation-defined choice over two steps.

---

Luckily, the set of values it describes already has a name in the Core Spec: the [arithmetic NaN](https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/syntax/values.html#arithmetic-nan).
It is defined as `±nan(m)` with `m ≥ canon_N`, and the upper bound `2^signif(N)` is already in the side-condition for definition of `nan(m)`.
This replaces both steps with one:

```
1. If number is NaN,
    1. Let f32 be an implementation-defined [=arithmetic NaN=] of size 32.
```

By doing so, the `[=signif=]` anchor can be removed since it was only used by the removed step.

---

P.S. I think it would helpful for readers to add a note under the step that repeats the definition, so they do not have to follow the link:

```
Note: An arithmetic NaN of size N is a floating-point value ±nan(m) with canon_N ≤ m < 2^signif(N).
```

I have left it out for now, but am happy to add it.

comment.body: Yes, surely no reason to block this PR.
